status_reason: Provisional: the target gases and the hot exhaust duct location are known, but duct temperature, concentration ranges and optical access are missing, and no supplied source covers gas-phase measurement in a hot duct.
answer: Test mid-infrared absorption with a PIR fiber probe, because the CO2 and CH4 gas bands lie between about 4 and 10 µm, inside the 3–17 µm PIR transmission range. Silica fiber probes cannot reach these bands. Duct temperature, concentration range and gas-interface design are not in the supplied sources, so this is a first assessment to be confirmed in the lab.

inline.headline: Test MIR absorption spectroscopy of CO2 and CH4 with a PIR fiber probe in the hot exhaust duct, starting with lab gas-cell trials
inline.probe: MIR fiber probe with a gas-sampling or optical-access interface (design to be confirmed; not covered by the sources)
inline.install: Hot exhaust gas duct at an optical access port; exact port and path length unknown
inline.not_final_because: The sources support MIR for these gas bands and PIR fiber range, but no supplied claim covers gas-phase absorption in a hot duct; temperature, concentration range, path length and fiber temperature rating are unknown.

problems.text: A silica fiber probe, including the high-temperature Al/Cu-coated silica option, transmits only 350–2400 nm and cannot reach the 4–10 µm gas bands.
The sources cover MIR for liquids, soft solids (ATR) and thin layers, but none covers gas-phase absorption in a hot duct, so the gas interface and optical path must be designed and tested.

Band positions are approximate: the CO2 window is printed at 3.7–4.5 µm and a hydrocarbon window at 3.0–3.7 µm, while the gas-band list gives 4–10 µm, so the exact CO2 and CH4 lines must come from lab spectra.
Exhaust temperature, dust load, duct dimensions and concentration range are not given, and the temperature rating of the PIR fiber is not stated in the sources.

methods.why: The CO2 and CH4 gas bands lie in the 4–10 µm region, inside the PIR fiber range, and MIR shows well-defined absorption peaks that need chemometric calibration.
The NIR evidence covers liquids, colloids, powders and scattering solids; no source supports NIR for gas bands in a duct.
Raman signals are weak and masked by laser scatter; no source supports Raman for gas in a hot duct.
Most chemicals do not fluoresce, and the cited fluorescence uses are biological; no source gives a fluorescence signal for CO2 or CH4.

questions.q: What are the duct gas temperature, pressure, and the CO2 and CH4 concentration ranges?
questions.why: These set the fiber exposure limits, the optical path and the calibration range; none are in the enquiry.

questions.q: What optical access is available at the duct (port size, path length across the duct, window material)?
questions.why: The interface decides the method and technique, and the sources say the task decides the interface.

questions.q: Is the exhaust gas dusty or wet, and how long must the probe run without service?
questions.why: Remote fiber placement keeps the spectrometer away from dust, but probe survival in exhaust is not covered by the sources.

questions.q: Can you provide an existing spectrum of the exhaust gas or of CO2 and CH4 standards?
questions.why: A spectrum shows whether the CO2 and CH4 features appear in the expected windows before any probe design.

questions.q: What accuracy, response time and independent reference method (laboratory gas analysis) are required?
questions.why: Reference values must be independent laboratory analyses, and the go or no-go decision depends on these criteria.

experiment.objective: Test whether MIR absorption through a PIR fiber sees CO2 and CH4 at concentrations and temperatures representative of the duct.
steps: Confirm with AFS the PIR fiber temperature rating and length suitable for the duct port.
Record MIR spectra of CO2 and CH4 reference gases at several concentrations in a laboratory gas cell coupled through PIR fiber, covering 3–17 µm.
Repeat the measurements at elevated temperature within the fiber's rated limit to check band shifts and intensity changes.
Identify key features in the 3.7–4.5 µm and 4–10 µm regions and check their overlap with the hydrocarbon window.
Build a chemometric model against independent laboratory gas analyses, validate on held-out spectra, and compare with the client's accuracy need.
references: AFS S01 p.5 (chemometric calibration and validation)
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client (accuracy, response time, temperature limit), not from the sources.

pathway.key_features: CO2 and CH4 gas bands in the 4–10 µm region; CO2 window printed at 3.7–4.5 µm and hydrocarbon window at 3.0–3.7 µm (approximate).
pathway.path_reason: Duct-condition gas data are needed before any path is justified; the lab test comes first.

multispectral.why: No supplied passage shows a complementary second method for gas-phase CO2 and CH4; a combination is only a hypothesis after a single-method test.
multispectral.test: If the single MIR model fails validation on the same data, test a second method against it, using synchronised data and the same validation set.

assumptions: The measurement is gas-phase absorption through an optical access port in the duct.
The CO2 and CH4 window positions are approximate until lab spectra are recorded.
Independent laboratory gas analyses are available as reference values.
Exhaust temperature, dust load and concentration range are unknown and not assumed.
